passage: In the reading room of the college library, two weeks before semesters, Rashmi pushed away her chemistry notes. 'I always freeze in exams, Yash. Always. My mind goes white.' Yash, who shared her table most evenings, tore a page from his notebook. 'Always? Let's test it. Write the exams where you didn't.' She rolled her eyes, but she wrote. Unit test in October: fine. The practical viva: fine, even good. Class 12 maths boards: fine. Then the freezes: first-semester organic chemistry, the entrance mock. She stared at the two columns. 'The fine ones... I'd done past papers under a timer. For the freezes, I'd only read notes.' Yash tapped the page. 'So it's not always. It's when you haven't practised against the clock.' Rashmi pulled the chemistry past papers out of her bag and set a forty-minute timer.

qa.q: Which exams did Rashmi freeze in?
qa.a: Rashmi froze in first-semester organic chemistry and the entrance mock.

qa.q: Why did 'I always freeze' feel true to Rashmi before the list?
qa.a: The freezes were so upsetting that they stood out in memory while the calm exams faded, so a few bad moments felt like the whole pattern.

qa.q: What did the two columns reveal that Rashmi could work on?
qa.a: They showed that the difference was timed practice: she froze when she had only read notes, so she started past papers against a forty-minute timer.

qa.q: How might Yash feel watching Rashmi set the timer?
qa.a: Yash probably feels glad that one torn page helped turn a fear into a plan, and may study better alongside her too.

grounding: Shows a student who believes she always freezes in exams listing the times she didn't, finding what was different and what to practise.

passage: Nineteen exams, Arnab. That's the number that changed it. Since you're recording this for the college radio, I'll start at the start. In second year I'd walk into an exam hall, see the first question, and my head would go blank. I told everyone, 'That's just Gopika. I always freeze.' Then the student counsellor asked me to bring a list: every exam I'd written in two years, and next to each, freeze or no freeze. I nearly didn't. When I did, there were nineteen exams. I'd frozen in four. Four! And all four had one thing in common: I'd stayed up all night before them. The other fifteen, I'd slept. So now, the night before an exam, I sleep, even if revision isn't finished. And I say, 'I sometimes freeze when I'm exhausted.' Less dramatic. But true.

qa.a: Gopika had frozen in four of the nineteen exams.

I'm Maria, and I share a room with Dilnaz in the women's hostel. Every exam season she says the same line: "I always freeze. I'll sit there and my brain will go white."

Last month, two weeks before semesters, she was saying it again when I handed her a pen. "Always? List the times you didn't."

She rolled her eyes, but she wrote. Statistics mid-term: fine. Economics viva: fine, even funny. Second-year finals: froze in one paper. I watched her add a column, "What was different?" Next to the good ones: "slept properly", "reached early", "started with a question I knew". Next to the frozen one: "stayed up all night, read notes in the corridor".

She sat back and stared at the page. "So I don't always freeze. I freeze when I don't sleep."

I can't say what she felt exactly. But the night before her first paper, she was asleep by eleven.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz write next to the frozen paper?
qa.a: "stayed up all night, read notes in the corridor".

qa.q: What does Dilnaz's line "So I don't always freeze. I freeze when I don't sleep" suggest about her thinking?
qa.a: She seems to have moved from a fixed rule about herself to a specific cause she can control. The counter-examples loosened the "always" and showed her what to work on.

qa.q: Why did adding the "What was different?" column help so much?
qa.a: It turned the list into clues: sleep, arriving early and starting with a known question went with the good exams. That gave Dilnaz concrete things to repeat.

qa.q: Why can Maria only guess at what Dilnaz felt?
qa.a: Maria sees the list, the stare at the page and the early night, but not what's inside. Maria reads the early sleep as a sign the lesson landed.

grounding: A roommate watches a student who believes she always freezes in exams list times she didn't and what was different, loosening the rule.

Monday: In the engineering college canteen, Karthik pushed away his dosa. "Thermodynamics on Saturday. I always freeze in exams, Sabina. Every single time."

Sabina stirred her tea. "Every single time? Name them."

Wednesday: Karthik sat in the library with a notebook, a bit annoyed that he'd agreed to do this. Exams in two years: fourteen. Froze: three. He looked at the three. All were first papers of the semester, all after cramming till 3 a.m. The eleven good ones: he'd done a timed practice paper the week before.

"Three out of fourteen," he told Sabina, sounding almost disappointed. "That's not always."

Saturday: The night before, he did a timed practice paper and slept at eleven. In the hall his hands shook when he saw question one. He skipped to question three, which he knew. By the time he came back, his head had cleared.

He didn't feel brave. He felt prepared.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel if she heard Karthik say he felt prepared, not brave?

passage:
I'm Samir, and in second year I had a rule about myself: I always mess up presentations. I believed it the way I believed the sun rises.

Before the final-year seminar, my friend Francis made me do something annoying. "List every presentation you've done since first year. Mark the bad ones."

There were eleven. Three were bad. Eight were fine, and two were actually good; the professor had said so.

Then Francis said, "Now, what did the three bad ones have in common?" I looked. For all three I'd made the slides the night before and never once said the talk out loud.

It was a shock. The rule wasn't "I always mess up." It was "I mess up when I don't rehearse." For the seminar I rehearsed three times: once to Francis, once to the mirror, once on the bus. It went fine.

qa.q: How many presentations had Samir done since first year?
qa.a: Samir had done eleven presentations.

qa.q: How did Samir feel seeing only three bad presentations out of eleven?
qa.a: Samir felt shocked and relieved, as the rule "I always mess up" didn't match the record.

qa.q: What did the counter-examples reveal Samir could work on?
qa.a: That the bad ones were never rehearsed, so Samir rehearsed three times before the seminar.

qa.q: How might Francis feel after the seminar goes fine?
qa.a: Francis would likely feel pleased that the annoying exercise worked, and proud of Samir.

Tutor's note, final-year engineering, 11 March.

Varun came to me convinced he "always blanks in vivas". He has one in two weeks and was talking about skipping it.

I asked him to test the rule. We listed every viva since first year: seven in total. He blanked in two. In five he answered most questions, including one where the examiner praised his circuit explanation.

Then we compared the two blanks with the five good ones. In both blanks, the examiner opened with a question outside the syllabus, and Varun froze trying to recall a perfect answer. In the good ones, he said, "Let me think aloud," and worked it through.

So the rule is not "always". It is "when the first question surprises me and I try to be perfect". We practised saying "Let me think aloud" to surprise questions, five times.

He will attend the viva. I'll ask him how it went.

Kashish

qa.a: Varun had done seven vivas.

qa.q: Why was Varun thinking of skipping the viva?
qa.a: Varun felt anxious and sure that he always blanks, so avoiding the viva seemed safer.

qa.q: What did comparing the good and bad vivas reveal?
qa.a: Blanks came when the first question surprised him and he chased a perfect answer; thinking aloud had worked, so they practised that.

Xin pushed a sheet of paper across the table. "Fine. Write down every exam since September. Mark the ones you froze in."
